title: Loss diagrams: logistic loss vs. hinge loss
intro: Probably the most conceptual topic of the course — but once you grasp this picture, you know exactly what logistic regression and SVMs are and why they behave differently. The charts below are interactive: move your mouse over them.

blocks.html:
We draw loss curves on a fixed kind of coordinate system: on the vertical axis the loss, on the horizontal axis the raw model output \( f(x) = w \cdot x + b \). Because we predict based on the sign, the vertical axis at zero splits the picture into two halves: on the left we predict class −1, on the right class +1.

We look at a single training example that belongs to class +1. Then the right half (positive output) is correct and the left half is incorrect. Note: this is different from the decision-boundary pictures of chapter 1 — here the axes are not two features, but raw output and loss, no matter how many features your model has. And this is the loss for one example; the total loss is the sum over all examples.

blocks.title: The 0-1 loss of one example (y = +1)
blocks.subtitle: Left (negative raw output): wrong → loss 1. Right: correct → loss 0.

sections.title: Why the squared loss fails for classification

blocks.html:
For linear regression the raw output is the prediction, and there the squared loss works fine: the further from the true target (here assumed 1), the higher the loss. But for a linear classifier that makes no sense: the sign has to be right, the distance to the target is irrelevant.

See the problem in the curve: the left arm is fine (mistakes are punished hard), but the right arm is disastrous — a large positive raw output means a correct, confident prediction, and the squared loss punishes exactly that with a high penalty. You would thus judge "perfectly good" models as bad during fitting. That is why we need special loss functions for classification.

blocks.title: Squared loss vs. the raw model output (y = 1)
blocks.subtitle: The right arm rises — correct, confident predictions get punished.

sections.title: The two stars: logistic loss and hinge loss

blocks.html:
The logistic loss (used by logistic regression) is in effect a smoothed version of the 0-1 loss: as you move right — the zone of correct predictions — the loss decreases gradually. The interpretation as "number of mistakes" is gone, but in exchange this loss can be minimised in practice.

The hinge loss (used by SVMs) has the same basic shape, but with one crucial detail: from raw output +1 onwards the loss is exactly zero and stays there — there is a "flat" section. When you predict an example correctly beyond a certain error margin, the example no longer contributes anything to the fit. This flat section is the key to support vectors in chapter 4.

blocks.title: All three classification losses together
blocks.subtitle: Move over the chart to read off exact values.

blocks.label: logistic loss
blocks.latex: L_{\text{logistic}}\bigl( y,\, f(x) \bigr) \;=\; \log\!\left( 1 + e^{-\,y\, f(x)} \right), \qquad y \in \{-1,\,+1\}
blocks.caption: The loss of logistic regression (for one example).

blocks.label: hinge loss
blocks.caption: The loss of SVMs — exactly 0 as soon as y·f(x) ≥ 1 (the "flat section").
The losses side by side, numerically
blocks.source:
import numpy as np

raw = np.array([2.0, 0.5, -0.5, -2.0])
y = 1  # the example belongs to class +1

hinge    = np.maximum(0, 1 - y * raw)
logistic = np.log(1 + np.exp(-y * raw))
zero_one = (np.sign(raw) != y).astype(int)

print(f"{'raw':>6} {'0-1':>4} {'hinge':>7} {'logistic':>9}")
for r, z, h, l in zip(raw, zero_one, hinge, logistic):
    print(f'{r:+6.1f} {z:4d} {h:7.3f} {l:9.3f}')

blocks.html: These two curve shapes are the essence of logistic regression and SVMs. Everything that follows — regularisation, probabilities, support vectors, kernels — builds on these diagrams.
